Diagnosis at discharge: Hepatitis B virus-related liver cirrhosis with portal vein thrombosis, portal systemic encephalopathy, and intracerebral hemorrhage.

The patient, a 14-year-old female, was admitted to our center due to recurrent palpitation and tremor. She was diagnosed with hyperthyroidism in another hospital, for which she had been prescribed methimazole primarily followed by propylthiouracil. Her thyroid function remained abnormal over the subsequent three years. All antithyroid drugs were discontinued for five months prior to her admission to our center.

Elevated TRAb levels were also detected. A point mutation in the TR β gene was identified in the patient and her father, indicating THR syndrome.

The patient's case was complicated by Graves' disease, and propranolol and methimazole were prescribed for treatment. The patient was discharged in stable condition and has since been followed up regularly. 

Discharge Diagnoses: 
- Toxic multinodular goiter complicated by Graves' disease

Discharge Medications: 
- Methimazole 30 mg/day
- Propranolol 60 mg/day

The patient is advised to continue taking prescribed medications and attend regular follow-up appointments.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:

This is a discharge summary for a postmenopausal woman in her 50s who was diagnosed with Stage IIB breast cancer and received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with a combination of DOC, pertuzumab, and trastuzumab after EC (every 3 weeks, 4 times) treatment. The patient experienced several symptoms during treatment, including grade 2 diarrhea, grade 1 fatigue, grade 1 edema, and grade 1 peripheral neuropathy. The patient's medical history included integration disorder syndrome, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia, all of which were well controlled by medication. The patient was a current smoker (10 cigarettes per day) and a social drinker with normal liver and renal function.

Summary of Treatment:

Dexamethasone, pegfilgrastim, metoclopramide, and Goshajinkigan, a herbal medicine, were administered to manage side effects such as taxane-associated acute pain syndrome and edema, peripheral neuropathy, and nausea. The patient also received 40 mg of the probiotic Clostridium butyricum MIYAIRI to prevent diarrhea, which was controlled with loperamide.
After the second cycle of EC and before the second cycle of DOC + pertuzumab + trastuzumab, the patient's serum triglyceride level mildly increased, then stabilized without any countermeasures. However, after the third cycle, the serum triglyceride level suddenly increased to grade 3 (770 mg/dL) without any symptoms. The fourth-cycle treatment was conducted, and sustained-release bezafibrate 200 mg was administered twice a day from the day, which resulted in a significant decrease in the serum triglyceride level to grade 1 (287 mg/dL) after 16 days. Bezafibrate administration was stopped on day 28 of the fourth cycle, and the level further decreased to the baseline level (212 mg/dL) on day 39.

Course After Chemotherapy:

Surgery was conducted on day 39 of the last chemotherapy cycle, and adjuvant chemotherapy consisting of pertuzumab and trastuzumab was resumed 52 days after the surgery. The lipid levels did not change during adjuvant chemotherapy. The patient experienced grade 1 aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and γ-glutamyltransferase elevation confirmed in the second cycle of EC and continued to be around the same level until the end of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. No other new medications were administered during chemotherapy.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with Stage IIB breast cancer with estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive, HER-2 overexpression positive, and Ki-67.

Condition at the Time of Discharge:

The patient's condition at the time of discharge was stable. The lipid level returned to a baseline level of 212 mg/dL, and the patient did not experience any significant side effects from chemotherapy.

Follow-up Care:

The patient will be monitored for any recurrence of breast cancer and will receive follow-up care according to the standard clinical practice guidelines.

The patient's final orthodontic treatment had satisfactory results with ideal overjet and overbite as well as achieving Class I canine and molar relation. The patient's long-term retention was planned to sustain the correction achieved in her orthodontic treatment. The patient was scheduled for periodic evaluations to minimize the chances of relapse.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 43-year-old male with primary hypothyroidism was admitted for evaluation of progressive fatigue, weakness, muscle and joint pain in the setting of recurrent fractures.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had been experiencing musculoskeletal pain in several locations including bilateral knees, ankles, left shoulder, left arm, and lower back which affected his overall functional status. He struggled to climb a flight of stairs, often grabbing the railing to pull himself up. A nuclear medicine bone scan showed abnormal uptake in bilateral ribs, vertebrae, right knee, hips, ankles, and feet. A lower extremity MRI showed stress fractures in left fibula, fifth metatarsal, and right tibia.

Course in Hospital:
The patient was started on calcitriol and phosphate supplements which significantly improved muscle weakness. Due to concern for TIO, a positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan with 68Gallium (68Ga)-DOTATATE was performed which showed multiple lytic osseous lesions with increased somatostatin positive uptake seen throughout pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet. However, after re-review with radiology, multiple areas of increased uptake were considered to be secondary to fractures, and left posterior acetabular lesion was presumed to be the tumor of interest given a remarkably higher standard uptake values (SUVmax) in this lesion compared to other lesions (SUVmax 20 vs. 4–5).

Procedure:
The left acetabular lesion was biopsied and pathology demonstrated a 1.4 cm phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor of the left acetabulum with uninvolved margins. The patient underwent radical resection of the tumor of the posterior left acetabulum with reconstruction of the posterior wall and posterior column of the acetabulum through a Kocher-Langenbach approach. His hip joint was able to be spared utilizing a 3D-printed custom bone cutting guide (CG) and intra-operative O-arm guided surgical navigation (Medtronic© Stealth) utilizing a navigated Sonopet Ultrasonic Bone Cutting Bovie (Stryker). The posterior wall and column of his acetabulum were constructed with a tantalum augment (Zimmer) and a pelvic reconstruction plate and screw construct (Synthes) after tumor removal.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged with normal phosphorus and FGF23 levels, pain-free left hip, no evidence of hardware complication, back to hiking, and walking on the treadmill. Clinical and radiographic follow-up at 6 months postoperatively found him to be pain-free in his left hip, with almost complete resolution of bone pain, and no recurrence of fractures. Phosphorus level also remained normal at 3.4 mg/dL 6 months after surgery.

A 67-year-old, right-handed female patient was admitted to the emergency department presenting with altered mental status. Neurologic examination was very limited secondary to sedation. Per family, the patient had a 2-week history of malaise, generalized weakness, headache, incontinence, and eventually altered mental status. On examination, her vital signs included temperature: 98.3°F, pulse: 99/min, BP: 201/94 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation: 98% after intubation. Initial laboratory work demonstrated a normal complete blood count (CBC) and normal coagulation. Blood chemistry was notable for an elevated calcium of 14.5 mg/dL. Liver function tests demonstrated an elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 208 U/L; renal function laboratories were within normal limits. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a white blood cell count (WBC) of 91 with a lymphocyte value of 90, and a protein of 32. CSF testing for herpes simplex virus, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcus, West Nile virus, and syphilis were all negative. Head computer tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) were negative. Electroencephalography (EEG) repeatedly showed generalized slowing. On day 2, MRI fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) showed abnormal posterior subcortical signal density with bilateral thalamic pulvinar involvement.

During the hospital course, the patient was admitted to the ICU and underwent aggressive blood pressure management. Her blood pressure was brought down to 140/57 mm Hg over 4 days. Her mentation slowly improved over 1 week; she was extubated on day 8. Repeat blood work showed a normal chemistry with a calcium of 7.4 mg/dL. Her ALP had decreased to 125 U/L. NMDA receptor antibody was negative both in serum and CSF. Prion study was negative with negative RT-QuIC and no 14-3-3 protein.

The patient was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, requiring further management. The patient neurologically continued to improve to a close to baseline state. She was discharged home after a 20-day stay in the hospital.

A 1-month postdischarge phone call revealed the patient had remained at her baseline mentation. Unfortunately, the patient eventually passed away from her pancreatic cancer 5 months later.
